text:
bob_cust: Hey team, our on-prem installer keeps failing during the bootstrap step. We see TLS handshake failures to model-registry and 403s to telemetry. This only happens inside our VPC/private cluster (we use split-horizon DNS).

bob_cust: Example from one node:```
$ curl -v https://model-registry.redwood.ai/v1/models/123
* Connected to model-registry.redwood.ai (10.0.2.5) port 443(#0)
* TLS 1.2 connection using ...
* TLS alert number 40
* SSL: TLS_v1_2 (IN), TLS handshake failure
* Closing connection 0
curl: (35) SSL handshake failed: SSL error in connection
```

alice_support: Thanks @bob_cust — sorry about that. A few quick clarifying Qs: 1) Are you routing outbound HTTPS through a corporate proxy (eg Zscaler) or doing direct NAT? 2) Can you paste a short portion of the installer log (the curl/wget lines) and the node OS image? 3) Do you have any SNI interception / TLS MITM on egress?

bob_cust: We have a TLS inspection appliance for some subnets, but the installer pods are on a workspace that should bypass the proxy. We suspect split-horizon DNS: internal DNS resolves model-registry.redwood.ai -> 10.0.2.5 (internal VIP) which is not reachable from the install host when it tries to egress through NAT. Installer logs:```
2024-06-08T14:23:12 boot: pulling https://files.pythonhosted.org/... -> failed (SSL handshake)
2024-06-08T14:23:13 telemetry: POST https://telemetry.redwood.ai/track -> 403
2024-06-08T14:23:14 model registry lookup model-registry.redwood.ai -> 10.0.2.5
```

deploy-bot: [deploy-log] installer-run-2024-06-08 started by bob_cust. Exit code 78. Logs uploaded -> https://priv-artifacts/redwood/installer/2024/06/08/installer-run-2024-06-08.log

carol_devops: Looks like a split-horizon / NAT mismatch. For the installer and runtime we recommend allowing egress by FQDN (443) to the public-facing endpoints rather than IPs. Minimal allowlist we usually provide:```
- pypi.org
- files.pythonhosted.org
- telemetry.redwood.ai
- auth.redwood.ai
- model-registry.redwood.ai
- model-shards.redwood.ai
- s3.amazonaws.com (for model shard hosting)
- ocsp.int-x3.letsencrypt.org (OCSP checks)
- kms.<region>.amazonaws.com (if using AWS KMS)
```
All on port 443; also allow port 80 for OCSP/CRL where applicable. If you have a TLS-inspection proxy, please ensure it either: a) has the Redwood CA pinned, or b) bypass rules for installer/runtimes so the TLS connection can use SNI to route correctly.

carol_devops: As a quick repro, can you try forcing DNS to the public IP from one node to see if the TLS handshake succeeds:```
# replace PUBLIC_IP with the registry's public IP
curl -v --resolve model-registry.redwood.ai:443:PUBLIC_IP https://model-registry.redwood.ai/v1/health
```
If that works then the issue is definitely the split-horizon mapping to an unreachable internal IP when egressing via NAT.

bob_cust: Tried the --resolve trick from a node; when forced to PUBLIC_IP it returns 200 and json {"ok":true}. So split-horizon is the root cause. Our networking team says they cannot change the internal mapping for other services.

alice_support: Ok — two pragmatic options: 1) Add allowlist entries and a proxy bypass for installer and runtime namespaces so egress goes direct to public endpoints. 2) Configure the outbound NAT to route requests for those internal-resolved IPs back to the internal network (if you want to keep internal mapping). The first is usually simpler.

dave_security: Also note security requirements: allow OCSP/CRL hostnames and STS/KMS endpoints used for auth. For AWS-based KMS/sts: allow kms.<region>.amazonaws.com and sts.amazonaws.com. Don't open 0.0.0.0/0 for all egress — prefer per-FQDN or CIDR for the known endpoints. Ensure SNI passthrough is preserved for these FQDNs so the server cert validation succeeds.

dave_security: A note on telemetry 403s — if your proxy injects headers or strips auth headers we will see 403 at our side. Please confirm the proxy is not removing Authorization or x-request-id headers for those calls.

bob_cust: Understood. Can you provide a short NetworkPolicy / iptables example we can give to networking? We use Calico, but our firewall team asked for a simple iptables snippet to test first.

carol_devops: Example (iptables NAT + allow outbound to FQDN via public IP — use this only for quick test):```
# resolve PUBLIC_IP ahead of time (nslookup on a node that sees public DNS)
iptables -I OUTPUT -p tcp -d PUBLIC_IP --dport 443 -j ACCEPT
iptables -I OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -j DROP # ensure only explicit allows work
```
K8s egress recommendation (Calico egress selector):```
apiVersion: projectcalico.org/v3
kind: GlobalNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-redwood-egress
spec:
  selector: app == 'redwood-installer'
  egress:
  - action: Allow
    protocol: TCP
    destination:
      nets: ['0.0.0.0/0'] # prefer FQDN-based egress with proxy bypass if possible
  order: 100
```
(Replace nets with specific CIDRs if your security team requires IPs.)

alice_support: I'll open an internal KB for the KB-able steps and include the exact host list + OCSP/KMS notes. @carol_devops can you capture any additional shard hosts we use for the specific model families (some models use different S3 buckets)?

carol_devops: Will do. Also recommend adding these to your allowlist: `eval-cache.s3.redwood-storage`, `token-introspect.auth.redwood.ai`. I'll post the exact bucket hostnames in the KB.

bob_cust: Great, thanks. Timeline: we're planning another install window tomorrow 09:00 UTC — can someone be on standby if we run into more TLS failures?

alice_support: Yes — I'll be on standby and will ping infra on-call. Please share the installer run id when you start (deploy-bot link helps). We can escalate to network ops if the workaround doesn't hold. :thumbsup:
